title: What are the CQRS trade-offs: benefits (independent scaling of reads/writes, optimized read models, simpler write logic focused on invariants, easier to add new query shapes without touching the domain) vs costs (eventual consistency between write and read models, data duplication, more code/infrastructure, projection rebuild complexity): and when should you NOT use CQRS (simple CRUD apps, low traffic, when strong consistency between write and read is required on every request, when the team doesn't need independent read/write scaling)?
shortTitle: What are the CQRS trade-offs and when should you NOT use CQRS
keyPoints: Benefits: independent scaling, optimized reads, simpler write logic, easy to add new query shapes without domain changes.
Costs: eventual consistency between write and read models, data duplication, more code and infrastructure.
Projection rebuild complexity: when a projection schema changes or a bug corrupts it, you must rebuild from source.
Do NOT use CQRS for simple CRUD where reads and writes share the same shape.
Do NOT use CQRS for low-traffic systems where the scaling argument disappears.
Do NOT use CQRS when every request needs strong read-after-write consistency with zero staleness.
CQRS is not all-or-nothing: apply it only to high-skew aggregates and keep the rest as plain CRUD.

s1_definition.oneliner: CQRS buys independent scaling and fast tailored reads at the price of eventual consistency, duplicated data, and more moving parts, so skip it for simple, low-traffic, strongly-consistent CRUD.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Independent scaling** – Read and write sides scale separately; in banking, reads outnumber writes so you scale read instances independently.
- **Optimized read models** – Each screen is backed by a projection shaped exactly for it, no joins, no aggregate loading.
- **Eventual consistency** – The read model updates after the write commits, so there is a brief staleness window.
- **Data duplication** – The same information lives in both the normalized write model and denormalized read models.
- **Projection rebuild** – When a projection schema changes or a bug corrupts it, you must rebuild it from the source of truth.
s1_definition.analogy: Running two separate counters at National Bank of India is powerful when the branch is huge and busy, but for a tiny village branch with five customers a day it is wasteful. You now need two sets of records that must be kept in sync, and for a brief moment after a transfer the display board might still show the old balance. If the branch is small, one combined counter is simpler and always perfectly up to date.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  CQRS Trade-off Decision:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Is read/write skew > 10:1?                 │
  │  Are read queries complex (multi-join)?     │
  │  Do you need independent scaling?           │
  └──────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────┘
             │ YES (any)        │ NO (all)
             ▼                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
  │  Consider CQRS   │   │  Stay with CRUD  │
  │                  │   │  Simpler, no     │
  │  Pick lightest   │   │  eventual        │
  │  form that works │   │  consistency     │
  └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘

  CQRS Spectrum:
  ┌────────┬────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
  │ Light  │ Medium     │ Heavy        │ Full         │
  │ Same DB│ Same DB    │ Separate DBs │ Event Sourced│
  │ sync   │ async      │ async events │ + separate   │
  │ proj   │ projection │              │ read store   │
  └────────┴────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The honest way to talk about CQRS is to lead with the trade-offs rather than treating it as a silver bullet. The benefits are real: independent scaling of reads and writes, optimized read models with no joins, simpler write logic focused purely on invariants, and the freedom to add new query shapes just by building a new projection. In banking where reads outnumber writes by fifty to one, these benefits matter enormously.

But the costs are equally real. Eventual consistency means a client who just wrote and immediately reads may see stale data, so the UI must tolerate that. Data duplication between normalized and denormalized models costs storage and risks drift. More code and infrastructure: ten classes instead of three. And projection rebuild is operationally complex when schemas change or bugs corrupt the read model.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj made this distinction explicitly. The branch-address reference data is a tiny table edited a few times a month, so he kept it plain CRUD and pushed back when someone proposed CQRS. The account-statement feature served millions of reads with a fifty-to-one skew and no strong read-after-write requirement, so there CQRS was clearly worth it. CQRS is not all-or-nothing: apply it only to high-skew, high-traffic aggregates that tolerate staleness, and keep simple, low-traffic workloads as plain CRUD.

Remember one sentence: CQRS buys independent scaling and fast tailored reads at the cost of eventual consistency, duplicated data, and more moving parts, so apply it only to aggregates where read-write divergence justifies the complexity.
